A [compressor](sound-compressor.qmd) turns loud sounds down. A **gate** does the opposite: it turns
*quiet* sounds down, all the way to silence. Below its threshold it's shut; when the sound gets loud
enough, it opens. A **transient shaper** changes the start of each note without touching the rest.
Both work on the *shape in time* of a sound, the [envelope](sound-envelopes.qmd), after it has been
recorded.

## The noise gate

<div class="sk" data-w="gate"></div>

The source is drum hits with **hiss and hum** mixed in, like a noisy recording or a guitar amp
buzzing between notes. The strip shows the level, the **threshold** (dashed) and where the gate is open
(shaded).

- **Threshold**: the gate opens when the level goes above it. Set it just above the noise and just
  below the quietest note you want to keep.
- **Attack**: how fast it opens. Too slow and the start of each hit is cut off.
- **Hold**: how long it stays open after the level falls, so it doesn't flutter.
- **Release**: how fast it closes. Too fast cuts off the tail of each note; too slow lets the noise
  back in.
- **Range**: how far it closes. −80 dB is silence; −12 dB just tucks the noise down, which sounds more
  natural.

Try **Clean up hiss**, then raise the threshold too far and listen to the hits getting chopped.

## The 80s gated snare

Choose **80s gated snare**: there is now a big reverb *before* the gate, and the gate is keyed by the
dry drums. Every hit gets a huge, explosive burst of reverb that stops dead a fraction of a second
later instead of fading. Phil Collins' "In the Air Tonight" made it famous in 1981 (the engineer Hugh
Padgham found it by accident on a talkback mic), and it's on half the pop records of the decade. Change
**Hold** to change the length of the burst.

## The transient shaper

The **transient** is the first few milliseconds of a sound: the stick hitting the drum, the pick on the
string. The rest is the **sustain** (the drum ringing, the room).

<div class="sk" data-w="transient" data-source="drums"></div>

- **Attack** up: every hit gets punchier and closer. Down: softer and further away.
- **Sustain** up: the ring and the room come forward. Down: the drums get tight and dry, as if the
  room were dead.

It does this with two envelope followers, one fast and one slow. Where the fast one is above the slow
one, a hit is starting: that gets the attack amount. Where it's below, the sound is ringing on: that
gets the sustain amount. Unlike a compressor, it doesn't care how loud the sound is, only whether it's
starting or fading. Try it on the **Synth riff** and on your **microphone** (clap).
